+# Are there mech-interp (Goodfire-style) solutions to the RR-calibration compute question?
+
+## Short answer
+
+Goodfire-style mechanistic interpretability is a specific tool: train a sparse autoencoder (SAE) on a neural network's internal activations to recover a sparse dictionary of interpretable "features," then steer those features to test causal hypotheses (Goodfire, https://www.goodfire.com/research/understanding-and-steering-llama-3). The method is motivated by superposition — the hypothesis that networks pack more features than neurons into an overcomplete set of non-orthogonal directions, which SAEs are designed to disentangle (Cunningham et al. 2023, https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.08600).
+
+The framer's core question — whether long MCMC chains are limited by hardware or by posterior geometry — is not a question about a learned neural network. It is settled by the effective-sample-size definition of autocorrelation (Stan Reference Manual, https://mc-stan.org/docs/2_31/reference-manual/effective-sample-size.html) and by the sampler-theory diagnosis that slow mixing "is frequently caused by an inappropriate selection of the proposal distribution" (Vrugt et al. 2009, https://research.wur.nl/en/publications/accelerating-markov-chain-monte-carlo-simulation-by-differential-). A GR4J forward model and an MCMC proposal have no internal activations for an SAE to decompose and no feature for steering to move. So for the literal "does a shit ton of GPUs fix τ" question the honest answer is no — mech interp is the wrong tool.
+
+But the framer's problem has two edges where Goodfire-style tools do apply: (a) the dominant modern rainfall-runoff model is now a learned neural network (an LSTM), and (b) the "geometry" behind long chains is exactly a "which directions actually matter" question, which is what features-plus-interventions are built to answer. Three concrete options follow.
+
+## SAE feature extraction on learned rainfall-runoff models
+
+LSTM rainfall-runoff models already exist and are known to have interpretable internals: Kratzert et al. found that individual LSTM memory cells track snow accumulation/melt and soil-moisture states, and that the cell states behave as storages (https://hess.copernicus.org/articles/22/6005/2018/; https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.07903). Goodfire's method turns this from hand-inspection into an automated sparse dictionary: an SAE trained on the cell-state activations recovers monosemantic feature directions, which is what Cunningham et al. showed for language models (https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.08600) and what King et al. have begun for geophysical MLPs, where SAEs reduced the average number of sensitive inputs per neuron by 33% and surfaced monosemantic features tied to temperature and fall-speed thresholds for precipitation phase (https://doi.org/10.1029/2025jh000769). The RR-specific payoff is to re-ask the framer's equifinality question at the feature level: which sparse features of the learned model are uniquely constrained by the runoff record, and which interchangeable feature sets reproduce it — a representation-level statement of Beven & Binley's equifinality (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/hyp.3360060305).
+
+## Feature steering to map the identifiable manifold
+
+Goodfire's steering intervenes on a single SAE feature and observes the downstream change (https://www.goodfire.com/research/understanding-and-steering-llama-3); the SAE-V work generalizes this into controlled interventions that validate a feature's causal role (https://arxiv.org/html/2502.06755v1). Applied to a differentiable RR model — an LSTM, or GR4J with the automatic differentiation Krapu et al. used for Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2021WR031377) — one could steer each feature and measure the change in simulated runoff or likelihood. The features that move the hydrograph are the directions the data identify; the features that do not are the equifinality directions that set τ. This is a causal map of the posterior geometry the framer identifies as the binding constraint (https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2003WR002378), produced by intervention rather than by assuming a proposal.
+
+## Active-subspace reparameterization of the calibration
+
+The mech-interp instinct — a few sparse directions carry all the information — has a non-neural cousin that already attacks MCMC directly: active subspaces identify the low-dimensional directions along which a forward model actually varies and separate "the low-dimensional subspace that is informed by the data" from "its orthogonal complement that is constrained by the prior" (Constantine, Kent & Bui-Thanh 2015, https://doi.org/10.1137/15m1042127). Running MCMC on the active variables while sampling the prior on the inactive ones is precisely the reparameterization the framer identifies as the real lever on long chains, and the subspace can be estimated from M gradient samples via finite differences at two forward evaluations each, regardless of input dimension (https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1506.04190). The open question for RR specifically is whether a single linear subspace survives the artificial multimodality that cheap fixed-step integrators inject into the posterior (Schoups et al. 2010, https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdfdirect/10.1029/2009WR008648).
+
+## What mech interp cannot touch
+
+Structural and input (rainfall) error — the modeling/likelihood changes Renard et al. describe as altering the posterior — and the data-availability limit are not feature-decomposition problems (https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2009WR008328). No SAE or steering intervention recovers parameters a record cannot identify.

+# Related problems that are compute constrained
+
+Related problems are counted here as compute constrained in the broad sense: (a) it is still open whether more parallel compute would change the answer, (b) compute is already known to bind there (marked "settled"), or (c) the answer takes long because its steps run one after another even though more hardware would not change the answer, only how soon it arrives.
+
+## Single-chain MCMC mixing
+
+A single Markov chain for a lumped conceptual model must run many serial iterations because posterior samples are autocorrelated; each step conditions on the previous state, and more parallel compute cannot shorten the chain's integrated autocorrelation time, only how fast samples accumulate.
+
+- **root_link:** Bears on the "what actually limits Bayesian calibration" half of the question — the single chain's autocorrelation is why lumped-model calibration is not compute-bound.
+- **compute_open:** none — more parallel compute buys samples-per-second but not a shorter autocorrelation time for a single chain, because τ (equivalently ESS = N/(1+2Σρ_k)) is set by target geometry and sampler, not by hardware (https://mc-stan.org/docs/2_31/reference-manual/effective-sample-size.html).
+- **sequential:** One converged posterior waits on one chain whose every step is a proposal from the current state plus a Metropolis accept/reject, and a single GR4J forward run is only a few thousand arithmetic steps per multi-decade daily record (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022169403002257), yet the chain must run on the order of up to 10^6 generations (DREAM(D)'s default maximum T_max; https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-15-3701-2011) to overcome autocorrelation, and the answer needs only a few independent chains (DREAM(ZS) uses N = 3–5; https://doi.org/10.1029/2011WR010608) for Gelman–Rubin checks, each keeping a tiny fraction of one GPU busy. These steps must run in order because each state conditions on the previous one, so the only way to run them at the same time is to run many independent chains in parallel, which pays off when the target is multimodal and chains are cheap (it buys coverage, not lower τ) — the nearest source that tried it is DREAM (https://research.wur.nl/en/publications/accelerating-markov-chain-monte-carlo-simulation-by-differential-).
+- **sources:** https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022169403002257 · https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-15-3701-2011 · https://mc-stan.org/docs/2_31/reference-manual/effective-sample-size.html
+
+## Ensemble / differential-evolution MCMC
+
+DREAM-style samplers run N chains simultaneously, generating each chain's proposal from differences of other chains' states; this improves exploration of multimodal/correlated hydrologic posteriors and enables Gelman–Rubin cross-chain diagnostics, and it is the one place where more GPUs change what gets sampled (by raising chain count) without lowering per-chain autocorrelation.
+
+- **root_link:** Bears on the "whether a shit ton of GPUs fixes it" half — GPUs buy more parallel chains (throughput and multimodal coverage), a real but bounded fix.
+- **compute_open:** More parallel compute buys simultaneous chains (ensemble members); standard DREAM runs N = d/2 to d (up to 2d) chains (https://doi.org/10.1029/2011WR010608), DREAM(ZS) needs only N = 3–5, and the largest reported run uses N = 25 chains on a 25-dimensional trimodal target (https://pure.uva.nl/ws/files/1553085/134391_wrcr13130_sup_0002_t02.txt), but it is still unknown whether chains beyond N = 25 further improve posterior coverage or mixing on higher-dimensional, more multimodal hydrology targets.
+- **sequential:** none — after burn-in the N chains' joint density factorizes and they are independent, so the ensemble already splits into N chains run simultaneously (https://doi.org/10.1029/2011WR010608).
+- **sources:** https://research.wur.nl/en/publications/accelerating-markov-chain-monte-carlo-simulation-by-differential- · https://doi.org/10.1029/2011WR010608 · https://pure.uva.nl/ws/files/1553085/134391_wrcr13130_sup_0002_t02.txt
+
+## Expensive distributed forward models
+
+For spatially distributed models with hundreds-to-thousands of parameters the forward-model cost dominates the calibration budget, and the workload decomposes into thousands of independent model runs that are embarrassingly parallel across chains and parameter sets; here compute is a genuinely binding constraint that parallelism relieves.
+
+- **root_link:** Bears on the "what actually limits Bayesian calibration" half — for expensive distributed models the forward-model cost, not mixing, is the binding limit.
+- **compute_open:** settled: more parallel compute is already known to bind and pay off here — the forward model dominates the budget (DREAM needed about 50 million surrogate-model evaluations to converge on a 241-parameter groundwater model, https://doi.org/10.1029/2011WR010608), distributed MT-DREAM(ZS) reports "spectacular performance improvement" on that same 241-parameter problem (https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2011wr010608), and GPU optimization of the MGB model yields up to 20× CPU speedup for calibration and 24× (CPU) / 65× (GPU) for simulations (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envsoft.2021.105271).
+- **sequential:** none — the calibration already decomposes into independent forward-model runs evaluated in parallel across chains and multiple simultaneous proposals, so it is embarrassingly parallel (https://doi.org/10.1029/2011WR010608).
+- **sources:** https://doi.org/10.1029/2011WR010608 · https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envsoft.2021.105271 · https://nhess.copernicus.org/articles/12/2411/2012/nhess-12-2411-2012.pdf
+
+## Large-sample multi-catchment calibration
+
+Calibrating many catchments (CAMELS provides 671 US catchments) is embarrassingly parallel because each catchment is independently calibratable, so GPU/cloud throughput directly determines how many catchments get a proper Bayesian treatment rather than point optimization.
+
+- **root_link:** Bears on the "whether a shit ton of GPUs fixes it" half — at CAMELS scale, throughput determines how many catchments can be afforded full Bayesian treatment.
+- **compute_open:** More parallel compute buys catchments given full Bayesian treatment instead of point optimization; the largest published set is CAMELS's 671 US catchments (https://hess.copernicus.org/articles/21/5293/2017/hess-21-5293-2017.html), and it is still unknown what extending full Bayesian treatment to all catchments above 671 (or globally) would change about large-sample hydrological conclusions.
+- **sequential:** none — the catchments are independently calibratable, so the study already splits into one independent calibration per catchment (https://hess.copernicus.org/articles/21/5293/2017/hess-21-5293-2017.html).
+- **sources:** https://hess.copernicus.org/articles/21/5293/2017/hess-21-5293-2017.html · https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/hyp.3360060305

1: # What actually limits Bayesian calibration of rainfall-runoff models — and whether "a shit ton of GPUs" fixes it
2: 
3: ## 1. My understanding, relayed before answering
4: 
5: Rainfall-runoff (RR) models map precipitation (and potential evapotranspiration) onto streamflow at a catchment outlet. The workhorse class for calibration studies is the lumped conceptual model — GR4J is the canonical example, with exactly **four** calibrated parameters and a simple production-store + unit-hydrograph structure evaluated a few thousand arithmetic steps per decade of daily data (Perrin, Michel & Andréassian 2003, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022169403002257). Bayesian calibration treats parameters as random and uses Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to sample the posterior p(θ | data).
6: 
7: Two facts dominate this literature:
8: 
9: 1. **Equifinality** — many different parameter sets reproduce the observed hydrograph almost equally well, so the posterior is broad, correlated, and often multimodal rather than a tight Gaussian around a single optimum. Beven & Binley (1992) state it directly: "within the limitations of a given model structure and errors in boundary conditions and field observations, different sets of values may be equally likely as simulators of a catchment" (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/hyp.3360060305).
10: 2. **Peculiar response surfaces** — hydrological model parameters are "highly correlated and interdependent," which is precisely what makes naive samplers mix slowly; summarizing/exploring the posterior is the stated bottleneck that "hindered widespread use of Bayesian techniques in hydrology" (Marshall, Nott & Sharma 2004, https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2003WR002378). MCMC inefficiency is "frequently caused by an inappropriate selection of the proposal distribution" — a geometric/algorithmic problem, not a hardware one (Vrugt et al. 2009, https://research.wur.nl/en/publications/accelerating-markov-chain-monte-carlo-simulation-by-differential-).
11: 
12: MCMC samples are autocorrelated. The information content of a chain of length N is the effective sample size ESS = N / (1 + 2Σρ_k), where ρ_k are lag autocorrelations; slow mixing inflates the integrated autocorrelation time τ and forces long chains to reach any target ESS (Stan Reference Manual, https://mc-stan.org/docs/2_31/reference-manual/effective-sample-size.html). The integrated autocorrelation time is defined as the number of correlated samples needed, on average, to produce one independent draw (LaplacesDemon IAT/ESS documentation, https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/LaplacesDemon/help/ESS.html). So "needs long MCMC chains" is a symptom of large τ — a statistical property — not directly a statement about hardware speed.
13: 
14: ## 2. Predictions (stated before checking)
15: 
16: - **P1:** For a single lumped conceptual catchment, one forward run is so cheap that the likelihood is effectively free; the binding constraint is τ (mixing), not FLOPs.
17: - **P2:** The "long chains" requirement is a property of posterior geometry (correlation/equifinality/multimodality) and, secondarily, of numerical implementation; it is reduced by better samplers/reparameterizations, not by more cores.
18: - **P3:** GPUs help only where the problem decomposes into independent units of work: many chains (ensemble MCMC), many particles (SMC), many catchments (large-sample), or many forward runs (GLUE / expensive models). They cannot shorten a *single* chain's autocorrelation.
19: - **P4:** There are genuinely compute-bound levels — expensive distributed/high-dimensional models and large-sample (CAMELS-scale) studies — where more parallel compute changes what is even attempted.
20: 
21: ## 3. Analysis
22: 
23: ### 3.1 Why chains are long: geometry and numerics, not throughput
24: 
25: The reason hydrology needed MCMC at all — and found it hard — is that the posterior of a conceptual RR model is difficult to summarize and explore because parameters are strongly correlated (Marshall et al. 2004, https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2003WR002378). Equifinality formalizes this as "equal finality": many parameter pathways reproduce the observed runoff (Beven & Binley 1992, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/hyp.3360060305). The DREAM paper's motivating diagnosis is that slow mixing "is frequently caused by an inappropriate selection of the proposal distribution," and its remedy is a self-adaptive differential-evolution proposal that tunes scale and orientation during the search — i.e., a better *algorithm*, not more *hardware* (Vrugt et al. 2009, https://research.wur.nl/en/publications/accelerating-markov-chain-monte-carlo-simulation-by-differential-).
26: 
27: Autocorrelation is the currency here: τ is set by the target's geometry and the sampler, and is invariant to how many parallel chains you run. Running more chains increases the number of samples per wall-clock second, but each chain still pays the same τ per independent draw. That is why "just add GPUs" is not, by itself, a fix for slow mixing — it changes throughput, not τ.
28: 
29: There is also a subtlety specific to hydrology: **cheap numerics corrupt MCMC**. First-order, explicit, fixed-step integration of water-balance dynamics makes the model "computationally cheap" (explicitly desirable for MCMC), but that cheapness introduces artificial bimodality in marginal posteriors and causes "slow convergence of the MCMC algorithm" plus unreliable Gelman–Rubin diagnostics (Schoups et al. 2010, https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdfdirect/10.1029/2009WR008648). # What actually limits Bayesian calibration of rainfall-runoff models — and whether "a shit ton of GPUs" fixes it

## 1. My understanding, relayed before answering

Rainfall-runoff (RR) models map precipitation (and potential evapotranspiration) onto streamflow at a catchment outlet. The workhorse class for calibration studies is the lumped conceptual model — GR4J is the canonical example, with exactly **four** calibrated parameters and a simple production-store + unit-hydrograph structure evaluated a few thousand arithmetic steps per decade of daily data (Perrin, Michel & Andréassian 2003, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022169403002257). Bayesian calibration treats parameters as random and uses Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to sample the posterior p(θ | data).

Two facts dominate this literature:

1. **Equifinality** — many different parameter sets reproduce the observed hydrograph almost equally well, so the posterior is broad, correlated, and often multimodal rather than a tight Gaussian around a single optimum. Beven & Binley (1992) state it directly: "within the limitations of a given model structure and errors in boundary conditions and field observations, different sets of values may be equally likely as simulators of a catchment" (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/hyp.3360060305).
2. **Peculiar response surfaces** — hydrological model parameters are "highly correlated and interdependent," which is precisely what makes naive samplers mix slowly; summarizing/exploring the posterior is the stated bottleneck that "hindered widespread use of Bayesian techniques in hydrology" (Marshall, Nott & Sharma 2004, https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2003WR002378). MCMC inefficiency is "frequently caused by an inappropriate selection of the proposal distribution" — a geometric/algorithmic problem, not a hardware one (Vrugt et al. 2009, https://research.wur.nl/en/publications/accelerating-markov-chain-monte-carlo-simulation-by-differential-).

MCMC samples are autocorrelated. The information content of a chain of length N is the effective sample size ESS = N / (1 + 2Σρ_k), where ρ_k are lag autocorrelations; slow mixing inflates the integrated autocorrelation time τ and forces long chains to reach any target ESS (Stan Reference Manual, https://mc-stan.org/docs/2_31/reference-manual/effective-sample-size.html). The integrated autocorrelation time is defined as the number of correlated samples needed, on average, to produce one independent draw (LaplacesDemon IAT/ESS documentation, https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/LaplacesDemon/help/ESS.html). So "needs long MCMC chains" is a symptom of large τ — a statistical property — not directly a statement about hardware speed.

## 2. Predictions (stated before checking)

- **P1:** For a single lumped conceptual catchment, one forward run is so cheap that the likelihood is effectively free; the binding constraint is τ (mixing), not FLOPs.
- **P2:** The "long chains" requirement is a property of posterior geometry (correlation/equifinality/multimodality) and, secondarily, of numerical implementation; it is reduced by better samplers/reparameterizations, not by more cores.
- **P3:** GPUs help only where the problem decomposes into independent units of work: many chains (ensemble MCMC), many particles (SMC), many catchments (large-sample), or many forward runs (GLUE / expensive models). They cannot shorten a *single* chain's autocorrelation.
- **P4:** There are genuinely compute-bound levels — expensive distributed/high-dimensional models and large-sample (CAMELS-scale) studies — where more parallel compute changes what is even attempted.

## 3. Analysis

### 3.1 Why chains are long: geometry and numerics, not throughput

The reason hydrology needed MCMC at all — and found it hard — is that the posterior of a conceptual RR model is difficult to summarize and explore because parameters are strongly correlated (Marshall et al. 2004, https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2003WR002378). Autocorrelation is the currency here: τ is set by the target's geometry and the sampler, and is invariant to how many parallel chains you run. Running more chains increases the number of samples per wall-clock second, but each chain still pays the same τ per independent draw. That is why "just add GPUs" is not, by itself, a fix for slow mixing — it changes throughput, not τ.

There is also a subtlety specific to hydrology: **cheap numerics corrupt MCMC**. ### Interventions

A key part of our research preview is the ability to surface causally-relevant aspects of the model's computation and intervene on them. These computational elements significantly impact the model's output, such that modifying them would lead to meaningful changes in result. To understand this process, we first need to explain how we introduce the SAE into model computations and perform interventions.

Remember that an SAE autoencodes a model's activations $x$ at some layer (layer 19, in our case). The SAE prediction $\hat{x}$ is imperfect, so there's an error term $\epsilon$. We want to intervene on SAE features, so let's make the dependence on $h$ explicit:

 \begin{aligned} x &= \hat{x} + \epsilon\\ &= f_{\mathrm{dec}}(h) + \epsilon. \end{aligned} 

So now if we change $h \rightarrow \tilde{h}$ (for instance by changing the value of a feature) we change the output of the SAE to $\tilde{x} = f_{\mathrm{dec}}(\tilde{h}) + \epsilon$. The error term $\epsilon$ is unchanged, so everything the SAE hasn't captured is unaltered by our intervention on $h$. We now insert the modified activations $\tilde{x}$ back into the model and continue inference through all the remaining layers to the model output.

...

The loss we found most effective is the logit of the predicted token minus the mean of the logits:

 \begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{attrib}} = \pi(\tau_t \mid \tau_{\lt t}) - \bar{\pi} \end{aligned} 

where $\tau_t$ is the t-th token, $\tau_{\lt t}$ are the tokens up to position t, $\pi(\tau)$ is the logit of token $\tau$, and $\bar{\pi}$ is the mean of the logits. The intuition for using logits rather than the log-loss is that the gradient of $\log p(\tau_t)$ combines both the gradient for features that promoted the chosen token, and for features that suppressed predictions of other tokens, which was confusing to interpret. We also obtained interesting results using contrastive explanations (i.e. gradient for the difference between a pair of tokens) but the UX flow was more complex. Many of our initial experiments with our R1 SAEs have focused on steering the model’s responses by altering the strength of particular features. While we haven’t yet systematically investigated their occurrence or causes, we wanted to share two insights into steering R1, which we haven’t encountered in non-reasoning models.

We usually steer a model (e.g. using Ember) starting from the first token of its response. However, naively steering R1 at the beginning of its chain of thought fails. Instead, we have to wait until after the model first begins its response with something like "Okay, so the user has asked a question about…" to steer effectively.

Our hypothesis is that phrases like “Okay, so the user has asked a question about…” were so common in the reasoning traces on which R1 was trained, that the model effectively treats it as part of the prompt. (Similar prefixes are extremely common in R1’s reasoning traces: more than 95% of its English reasoning traces begin with "Okay,"). We observed a strong feature distribution shift between the prompt (including this prefix to the thinking trace), the thinking trace, and the assistant’s response.

When we steer a model, we vary the strength of the feature(s) we’re manipulating, thus controlling how salient that feature is to the downstream model output. # Do internals of neural networks make sense in the context of hydrology?

Presentation at the AGU 2018 Fall Meeting on experiments regarding the interpretability of LSTM states.

#### Abstract

In recent years, neural networks gained a new wave of popularity in many application domains, such as computer vision or natural language processing. However in applied environmental sciences, like rainfall-runoff modelling in hydrology, neural networks tend to have a rather bad reputation. This can be attributed to their black-box-ness and the difficulty or impossibility to understand network internals leading to a prediction.

In this study, we tackle this criticism and show how recent advances and methods in the area of interpretable machine learning allow for deeper analysis of network internals. As an example we use the Long Short-Term Memory network (LSTM) for the task of rainfall-runoff modelling. LSTMs are a special kind of recurrent neural network architecture and, as the name suggests, are able to learn short- and long-term dependencies between inputs and outputs due to special memory cells. This property is especially appreciable in hydrology, where outputs of the system tend to have a long memory. Kratzert et al. (2018) confirm this and have recently shown that LSTMs can achieve competitive results compared to the well established Sacramento Soil Moisture Accounting model, coupled with the Snow-17 snow module.

In this study, we explore the internals of trained networks for different basins from the publicly available CAMELS data set, also utilizing remote sensing data of soil moisture, snow cover and evapotranspiration fluxes. We show that LSTMs internally learn to represent patterns that match our understandings of the hydrological system. In snow-driven catchments e.g. the network develops special memory cells that mimic conceptual snow storages with annual dynamics, as known from process-based catchment models.

In general, we anticipate that our findings can increase the trust in the application of neural networks in environmental sciences. We however stress, that expert knowledge on the modeled system is inevitable and still remains an important quality against black-box-ness.

## 3.5 A hydrological interpretation of the LSTM

To round off the discussion of this manuscript, we want to come back to the LSTM and try to explain it again in comparison to the functioning of a classical hydrological model. Similar to continuous hydrological models, the LSTM processes the input data time step after time step. In every time step, the input data (here meteorological forcing data) are used to update a number of values in the LSTM internal cell states. In comparison to traditional hydrological models, the cell states can be interpreted as storages that are often used for e.g. snow accumulation, soil water content, or groundwater storage. Updating the internal cell states (or storages) is regulated through a number of so-called gates: one that regulates the depletion of the storages, a second that regulates the increase in the storages and a third that regulates the outflow of the storages. Each of these gates comes with a set of adjustable parameters that are adapted during a calibration period (referred to as training). During the validation period, updates of the cell states depend only on the input at a specific time step and the states of the last time step (given the learned parameters of the calibration period).

Figure 14 Boxplot of the NSE of the validation period for our three Experiments and the benchmark model. The NSE is capped to −1 for better visualization. The green square diamond marks the mean in addition to the median (red line).

In contrast to hydrological models, however, the LSTM does not “know” the principle of water/mass conservation and the governing process equations describing e.g. infiltration or evapotranspiration processes a priori. Compared to traditional hydrological models, the LSTM is optimized to predict the streamflow as well as possible, and has to learn these physical principles and laws during the calibration process purely from the data.

Finally, we want to show the results of a preliminary analysis in which we inspect the internals of the LSTM. Neural networks (as well as other data-driven approaches) are often criticized for their “black box”-like nature. However, here we want to argue that the internals of the LSTM can be inspected as well as interpreted, thus taking away some of the “black-box-ness”.

Figure 15 shows the evolution of a single LSTM cell (c t; see Sect. 2.1) of a trained LSTM over the period of one input sequence (which equals 365 days in this study) for an arbitrary, snow-influenced catchment. We can see that the cell state matches the dynamics of the temperature curves, as well as our understanding of snow accumulation and snowmelt. As soon as temperatures fall below 0 ∘ C the cell state starts to increase (around time step 60) until the minimum temperature increases above the freezing point (around time step 200) and the cell state depletes quickly. Also, the fluctuations between time steps 60 and 120 match the fluctuations visible in the temperature around the freezing point. Thus, albeit the LSTM was only trained to predict runoff from meteorological observations, it has learned to model snow dynamics without any forcing to do so.

...

An entirely justifiable barrier of using LSTMs (or any other data-driven model) in real-world applications is their black-box nature. Like every common data-driven tool in hydrology, LSTMs have no explicit internal representation of the water balance. However, for the LSTM at least, it might be possible to analyse the behaviour of the cell states and link them to basic hydrological patterns (such as the snow accumulation melt processes), as we showed briefly in Sect. 3.5. We hypothesize that a systematic interpretation or the interpretability in general of the network internals would increase the trust in data-driven approaches, especially those of LSTMs, leading to their use in more (novel) applications in the environmental sciences in the near future.
